expectations.text: Output flags the bipartite projection pathology (clique inflation, co-membership artifacts, inflated clustering)
expectations.evidence: Issue 1 explicitly describes how large projects create cliques, calls it 'an artifact of co-membership, not evidence of a tight-knit collaboration group,' and states it 'will inflate clustering coefficients, inflate modularity scores, and bias community detection toward absorbing those large-project cliques.'

expectations.text: Output recommends SDSM or FDSM backbone extraction specifically — NOT the disparity filter (which ignores bipartite structure and is wrong here)
expectations.evidence: Response names both methods explicitly: 'The standard method for bipartite projections is the SDSM (Stochastic Degree Sequence Model) or the FDSM (Fixed Degree Sequence Model).' The disparity filter is never mentioned. The bipartite-specific rationale is given.

expectations.text: Output mentions direct bipartite community detection as an alternative (bipartite SBM, biSBM, graph-tool bipartite)
expectations.evidence: Section 'If you want a more principled approach' states: 'since your data is bipartite, you can skip projection entirely and run a bipartite SBM directly on the person × project graph' with working graph-tool code using pclabel.

expectations.text: Output does NOT simply validate the Louvain-on-projection plan without warnings
expectations.evidence: Opening says 'on the right track conceptually, but there are two issues to fix before running Louvain — one that will meaningfully distort your results.' Concerns are co-presented with the partial acknowledgment, not afterthoughts.

expectations.text: Output explains why edge weights from bipartite projection are not the same as relationship strength (co-membership count confounds project size and individual activity)
expectations.evidence: Project-size confounding illustrated with 40-employee example. Individual-activity confounding addressed through SDSM/FDSM null framing. Both confounds substantively covered.
